prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit the ubiquitin-proteasome system to remove selected proteins.

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is the one shortlisted achievement that all eight of us ranked, and six placed it in the top three. That breadth matters more to me than my own opening first choice. Chemically it replaces occupancy-driven inhibition with induced proximity: a bifunctional molecule forms a ternary complex whose cooperativity, geometry and kinetics determine whether a protein is ubiquitinated and destroyed. That is a physical-chemical principle, with a large mechanistic literature on ternary-complex thermodynamics, and it has produced a new modality now in many clinical programmes. Crews and Deshaies proposed and demonstrated the first PROTACs, and Ciulli's VHL ligands and structural work made the approach rational and general. Two decades of independent confirmation make the maturity case solid.
statement.case_against: The credit story cannot be made clean with three names. The molecular-glue lineage (Handa and Ito on cereblon as the thalidomide target, plus Gray, Sakamoto and Kim) is a distinct discovery, and a PROTAC-only prize would leave it out. Clinical benefit is also still maturing, with few approved degraders, so recognition could be criticised as slightly early. Finally, my own opening first choice, phase separation (B045), is a more purely physical-chemical concept that I fear is underrepresented on the shortlist, but its maturity is genuinely contested and only three of us ranked it, so I do not think it can carry the prize this year.

responses.point: Linke proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa, framing induced proximity as one principle spanning PROTACs and glues, and notes that the PROTAC concept and the thalidomide-cereblon mechanism are separable.
responses.response: I agree the two lineages are separable, and that is why I hesitate to fold them into a single citation by choosing Handa. Handa identified a target of an existing drug, whereas Ciulli built a general design method for synthetic degraders. A citation on designed degraders is more coherent with Ciulli, and the glue story can be acknowledged in the scientific background. I would not object strongly to Handa if the committee prefers the broader induced-proximity framing, but then I would want that choice to be explicit and not an accident of a three-name limit.

responses.point: Aili ranks B014 first, honours the PROTAC core of Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, and accepts that glue degraders are partly left out. He also ranked lipid nanoparticles (B021) second.
responses.response: I largely agree on B014 and the PROTAC-core trio. On B021, I ranked it second myself, but I now think the credit is too diffuse across Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and the 2023 Medicine prize on nucleoside modification makes the framing risky. I would rather hold it as a strong alternative for a later year than split our votes between two drug-delivery-flavoured topics.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing (B042) first as a chemically elegant, mature application of deaminase chemistry with clinical use, and ranks PROTACs second.
responses.response: I take the chemical argument for base editing seriously and I ranked it fourth. My reservation is that the committee must show it is a distinct chemical invention beyond the 2020 CRISPR prize, and that the Nishida and Kondo parallel work complicates attribution. PROTACs carry less of that precedent risk, though I accept that if the committee judges the CRISPR concern manageable, Liu with Komor and Gaudelli is a credible competitor.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range protein electron transfer (B025) first as an overdue, mature, mechanistically clear achievement, and ranked phase separation last-ish at eighth.
responses.response: The electron-transfer work is conceptually beautiful and mature, but it has support from you alone, so I cannot see how it builds a majority this year. On phase separation I understand your doubt; the equilibrium-versus-active-state debate is real, and I share it. Still, I would not dismiss the underlying thermodynamic framework, which is why I keep B045 as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a prize on the PROTAC concept (Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli) or a broader induced-proximity prize that includes the cereblon glue mechanism (Handa).
Whether limited clinical approval of degraders makes recognition premature compared with base editing, which has clearer therapeutic outcomes.
Whether the contested equilibrium nature of cellular condensates is resolved enough to revisit B045 in a later round.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work in the same research area as lipid-based candidates (B021) and phase separation (B045) in a general sense and sit on the committee with Lund colleagues Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, but I have no stated personal or institutional tie to any credited name that would require recusal.
